review.summary: This PR adds a reflection-based zero test for the `ir` package and makes accessors safe to call on zero values. The mechanical pattern (`var slice T; if !zero { slice = ... }; return seq.NewFixedSlice(slice, ...)`) is applied consistently and is straightforward to verify. The main correctness concern is `(*File).AllMembers()` on a nil receiver: it returns an `iter.Seq` that wraps a nil inner `iter.Seq[*rawMember]` via `iterx.Map` — the test does not actually iterate function-typed returns, so a panic on consumption could slip through. Secondary concerns are minor: a few defensive patterns are awkward (`var imp imports; imp.Directs()` heap-escapes a synthetic value when a `var i *imports` + the already-nil-safe `Directs` would do), the `IsAny` short-circuit duplicates checks that other methods now centralize via `IsZero`, and the test has a shadowed loop variable. None of the new nil-guard patterns introduce regressions for the non-zero path; behavior is preserved.

issues.description: (*File).AllMembers on nil receiver returns an iter.Seq wrapping a nil inner Seq; iteration will likely panic
issues.detail: When f == nil, raw is left as the zero-value iter.Seq[*rawMember] (a nil function). It is then passed to iterx.Map, which returns a new Seq that, when consumed, will invoke the nil source Seq and panic with a nil-function-call. The new TestZero never actually iterates function-typed returns (it explicitly `continue`s on reflect.Func), so this regression is not caught by the new test. Either short-circuit with an empty iter.Seq (`func(yield func(Member) bool) {}`) when f == nil, or have iterx.Map tolerate a nil input Seq, and add a test that actually consumes the iterator on a zero receiver.

issues.description: TestZero skips function-typed returns, so iter.Seq accessors on zero values are not exercised
issues.detail: In testZeroAny, the inner loop does `if r.Type().Kind() == reflect.Func { continue }` for each return value. AllMembers (and any future iter.Seq accessor) returns a function; the test asserts nothing about it. Combined with the AllMembers nil-Seq issue above, this means the test's claim of "accessors do not panic" is only true for non-iterating callers. Either call the returned Seq with a yield that returns false immediately, or special-case iter.Seq the way Indexer is special-cased via Len().

issues.description: Imports() and TransitiveImports() construct a synthetic local `imports` value just to call a method that already handles nil
issues.detail: `imports.Directs` and `imports.Transitive` were both updated to handle a nil *imports. The caller in *File could simply be `var i *imports; if f != nil { i = &f.imports }; return i.Directs()`. The current form (`var imp imports; ...; return imp.Directs()`) forces the local to escape to the heap because Directs closes over the receiver, and it muddles intent — the reader has to verify that a zero `imports` value also produces empty results, in addition to the already-verified nil-receiver path.

issues.description: Type.IsAny short-circuits with !t.IsZero() but most peers route through their own zero-safe accessors
issues.detail: Other Type methods in this diff use `if !t.IsZero() { ... }` only to set a local slice/value, then fall through to a uniform return. IsAny instead inlines the check: `return !t.IsZero() && t.InternedFullName() == t.Context().session.builtins.AnyPath`. This is correct but stylistically inconsistent with the rest of the file's pattern, and if `t.Context()` is ever extended to return a non-nil sentinel for zero, the precedence here is harder to audit. Consider matching the local-variable pattern or pushing the zero check into Context/session access.

issues.description: Loop variable `i` is shadowed inside testZeroAny
issues.detail: `for i := range ty.NumMethod()` declares `i`, and the inner `for i, r := range returns` shadows it. Harmless today because the outer `i` is unused after the inner loop, but it is a readability nit that linters will flag (govet/shadow). Rename to `idx` or `ri`.

issues.description: Repeated `var slice T; if f != nil { slice = ... }; seq.NewFixedSlice(slice, ...)` pattern duplicated ~9 times in ir_file.go
issues.detail: Every top-level accessor (Types, AllTypes, Extensions, AllExtensions, Extends, AllExtends, Services, Symbols, Imports, TransitiveImports) repeats the same five-line incantation. A small generic helper such as `func nilSafeSlice[T any](f *File, get func(*File) []T) []T` would collapse each accessor to a single line and make the nil-safety guarantee uniform. Not blocking, but the duplication is the kind of thing that makes future changes drift.

issues.description: FeatureSet on nil File uses an explicit empty-struct early return while peers use id.Wrap with a zero id
issues.detail: `if f == nil { return FeatureSet{} }` is correct but inconsistent with neighbors like Options() which build a zero id and call `id.Wrap(f, options).AsMessage()`. If `id.Wrap(nil, zeroID)` produces a zero FeatureSet (very likely given the test passes), this branch is unnecessary. If it does not, then the inconsistency is itself worth a comment so readers know why FeatureSet needs the early return.

issues.description: ImportFor is not visibly nil-guarded in the diff
issues.detail: The diff guards every other top-level *File accessor against a nil receiver but does not touch ImportFor (line ~199). If ImportFor dereferences f (e.g., f.imports), it will panic on the zero pointer — but the new TestZero claims to exercise all 1-arg accessors. The test's `m.Func.Type().NumIn() != 1` filter excludes ImportFor because it takes an argument, so the gap is invisible to the new test. Confirm ImportFor is already nil-safe or add a guard for consistency.

dissents.topic: Whether AllMembers needs an actual fix or just a test

positions.position: The fact that a consumer of `(*File)(nil).AllMembers()` would panic is a real regression; the production path must be safe, and the test must consume the iterator to prove it.

If no caller invokes AllMembers on a nil *File today, this is a latent issue that can be filed and fixed in a follow-up. The PR's stated goal is parity with the ast zero test, not exhaustive iter-safety.
Push nil-safety into the leaf method (`imports.Directs` already handles nil); callers should just pass `nil` through. The current double-guard in *File methods is redundant.
Each *File method should be self-evidently safe without requiring the reader to verify the callee's nil semantics. The duplication is cheap insurance and survives refactors that move the leaf method.

dissents.topic: Reflection-driven zero test vs explicit per-type tests

positions.position: Reflection covers every accessor on every type at minimal cost and will keep covering new accessors as they are added — exactly what a zero-invariant test should do.

Reflection-based tests obscure which accessor failed, mishandle generics like `Ref[T]`, and silently skip whole categories (variadic, methods-with-args, functions returned from accessors). Explicit per-method tests, even if verbose, catch more and document the contract.
